blocks.p: I always ground my thoughts in the Polyvagal Theory primary source teachings. But fawn and appease are one area where I split off from the polyvagal orthodoxy. I deviate a bit from the official Polyvagal Institute and Dr. Porges doctrine here, so let me lay out how I see it.

In the book Our Polyvagal World, if I remember right, Dr. Porges and his son lay out fawning as flight and fight plus shutdown. But flight and fight plus shutdown is also freeze. So in very generic terms, they're suggesting that freeze and fawn have the same underlying autonomic activation. I personally don't like that.

To me, fawning is a behavior. It's something we'd recognize as a behavior, or a way of thinking: prioritizing somebody else, making sure their needs are met, as a way to placate them. That's a specific behavior, and I think it comes from shutdown.

I would argue that fawning is an adaptation to chronic, deep, severe shutdown or freeze activation. I look at it this way: someone is in a severe situation, something they cannot escape, like an abusive home or a hostage situation. Their state is chronically in shutdown or freeze, and I'd argue there's got to be a lot of shutdown in there. To adapt to that state, get their needs met, and reduce the amount of life threat in the situation, they fawn.

That's how I conceptualize it, because someone could have flight, fight, and shutdown active at the same time and not fawn. So it doesn't make sense to me that fawning and freeze have the same underlying neural pathways, unless we look at fawning as a behavioral adaptation to shutdown or freeze.

Same thing with appeasement, which I'm a little more on board with. Appeasement is, again, very contextually driven and behaviorally focused. The context would again be a situation they cannot escape. They can't fight, they can't run away, and shutting down won't work, because they won't get their needs met. They'll die.

In the book, appeasement is conceptualized as a combination of all of the states active at the same time, particularly in a situation like a hostage or kidnapping situation where they can't escape. Appeasement is a general set of behaviors. Someone appeases to reduce the potential life threat from the captor, and the appeasement also helps them get their needs met.

I would argue that appeasement comes from significant freeze or shutdown, and more shutdown, personally. When someone appeases or fawns, they could be acting in ways that are very much not in alignment with their true values. They're pretty disconnected from themselves at that point. To me, that means there's a ton of shutdown, and probably dissociation, which leads to these behaviors to get their needs met.

So could fawning or appeasing be a way to lessen the other person's defensive state, in your own interest? Exactly. These are strategies. Nobody is blueprinting this stuff out. They do what they have to do to survive the situation.

Appeasement in particular does seem to come with some safety activation. The person who can appease can use all of their states in these situations. They can come across as a friend or an ally to the captor: "I'm on your team. I'll help you hide from the police. I'll lie for you." Outside of that situation, that person would probably never think of doing those things, or feel good or proud about it. But in that context, those behaviors reduce the danger, the literal danger. They might help the captor's fight activation, probably their rage, come down enough that the person who is appeasing or fawning can get through the day.

So appeasement needs some social activation and some thinking available, and fawning may be different. With appeasing, I don't think it's a true, socially connected empathy. I don't think it's a true ventral vagal state. It's a pseudo connection, a fake connection. Or maybe the person does truly feel it. I don't know. I can't get into that part. But regardless, there does seem to be some ventral activation in there, enough to come across as a friend.
With fawning, it's not friendship. It's more like: I'm invisible. I'm not a threat. Don't pay attention to me.

The person receiving appeasement is being co-regulated by it, to some extent. If someone can smile at their captor or use their vocal prosody to calm them down, there has to be some ventral activation. But it's very much a one-way thing, I think. The person appeasing is getting their needs met, but they're not receiving co-regulation. It's "I'm giving you this." The captor or the abuser is receiving it, not consciously. They're not feeling empathy and love. It's not like that. But their defensive activation has to come down enough to get through that situation.
I don't know how to talk about this honestly, so I'll try. This is my assumption. I have no evidence for it. It's just how I think about it.

When we truly shut down, we collapse. We play dead. We cannot survive in that state. When we get deep enough into shutdown, there's dissociation. We disconnect from ourselves, and in severe cases, that could lead to dissociative identity disorder, or to derealization and depersonalization: really just disconnected from the self. But we still have to function. We still have to get our needs met. We can't live in a truly dissociated state very long at all. So human bodies in particular seem to have this ability to disconnect from what's happening. Even though it's a huge shutdown, somehow we can dissociate and then keep going.

And through that dissociation, we can take on what looks like a new personality. The person who's appeasing is so disconnected from their authentic self that they have to take on a new personality, a new system of values, a new way of thinking, feeling, and acting, in order to survive the situation. I think the same thing is true for someone who's fawning. They're deeply disconnected from their grounded, true self. I don't love that phrase, but I don't know how else to say it.

So once you get deep enough into shutdown, or deep enough into dissociation, you still have to get your needs met. You still have to go to work. You still have to go to school. You still have to survive some situation that's horrible. To me, it acts almost like a clean slate. It's not, but it's almost like: here's version one of me. I can't be this in this situation. So shutdown wipes that away. And here's version two, which is very compromised and is now appeasing or fawning, because I have to survive. But this is not me.

Once I get out of that situation, once I can get help and self-regulate, version two goes away, and we're back to version one. But now version one, this true self, has all this shutdown it has to deal with, all the pain it went through and dissociated from. That's where a whole new layer of self-regulation has to come in.

If someone is well regulated, they would feel a potential predator and push back. But if it's a situation they can't escape, or if they were raised in a situation they couldn't escape, couldn't fight from, couldn't even successfully shut down in, what other option do they have but to give themselves this dissociative blank slate and bring in a new personality? Sometimes I do think it is literally a new personality. But it's there to get through the day, to get through until they get to safety. It's almost like a reset. Version two. But version one is still there, way deep down, and we have to go through version two to get back to version one.
That's just me. That's just the way I think about it. I have no polyvagal evidence to back it up. Maybe it's better as a metaphor.
How does this relate to getting unstuck and recovering? I wish I had a great answer. I've worked with a couple of people who have severe dissociation.

My assumption is that for someone in version two, with severe dissociation and an almost new personality, there isn't a whole lot of state exploration at first. They need literal safety. Once they have literal safety, would they be able to self-regulate? They'd have to come out of that severe dissociation first and reconnect with their body. And then, well, now we have to deal with all the shutdown, and that's going to be severe, because it's probably connected to numerous longstanding traumatic incidents. And it probably wouldn't even be just shutdown. There'd probably be a ton of freeze too.
So the order would look something like this:

ol: Slowly reconnecting with the present moment. Probably not with a lot of safety yet, but can we reconnect with just the literal, objective world?
Slowly building toward the internal world.
If we can do that, starting some self-regulation work.

blocks.p: That would probably be a long process.

One client comes to mind. She had severe dissociation, and with good cause. We would meet, and later on she'd say, "I have no idea what we talked about." I couldn't tell, because she was so functionally good at it. She could come across like she was here, but she wasn't. We'd meet the next week and she'd say, "I remember coming in here, but beyond that, I don't know what we talked about."

Her dissociation was so high that we just had to practice literally connecting to what was happening in the room. What colors do you see? What can you touch? Sensory kinds of things. That was a process, and it took a while. Then we worked on feeling actual safety, and that was quite a challenge, but she finally identified a blanket that felt good, so we felt that mindfully. From there, we built into other safety pieces, and some actual self-regulation.

She got to a point where she was much more empowered. She was going to college. She was present. She was able to put boundaries in. She made huge progress. But the point is, it started with: can we just be present? Not even a deep mindful exploration. Just: are you here or not? Can you name things? Can you feel things? Tactically, I have my fidget basket for that.
Fawn and appeasement are areas where I tend to deviate from the official Polyvagal teachings. I see them as behavioral adaptations to a prolonged, severe, dissociative shutdown or freeze state.
